title: How Does the Iran War End? | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: CFR president Michael Froman argues Trump faces only three unattractive exits from Operation Epic Fury — dramatic escalation, deescalation that looks like capitulation, or continuation of the current messy stalemate — and that the stalemate is the most likely outcome. He handicaps duration with the Gott rule (even odds the five-month-old Hormuz stalemate runs through end-2026) and notes prediction markets independently put 50 percent on Strait of Hormuz commercial traffic returning to normal by year-end.

insights.claim: President Trump's realistic choices for ending the Iran war reduce to three unattractive options — dramatic escalation, conciliatory deescalation, or continuation of the current messy stalemate — and he has so far tried a middle course of simultaneous tit-for-tat strikes and new deal offers.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Gives a clean three-branch decision tree for pricing Gulf and oil risk: only the escalation branch is a genuine tail event.
insights.quote: The choice now before President Donald Trump may be to pick between the lesser of three unattractive options: a dramatic escalation, a conciliatory deescalation, and a continuation of today’s messy stalemate.
insights.locator: Much of the commentary on the war in Iran

insights.claim: Trump is reportedly giving serious thought to restarting sustained, high-intensity strikes akin to the opening of Operation Epic Fury, saying Iran hasn't received enough pain yet, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio has floated a strategy of 'a head for an eye.'
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Escalation rhetoric from both the president and the secretary of state is a live near-term catalyst for oil and shipping-insurance repricing.
insights.locator: The first approach would be to shoot our way out

themes.theme: Escalation option and its second-order targets

insights.claim: An escalation strategy would hit Iranian critical infrastructure — oil and gas facilities, power plants, transportation infrastructure and desalination plants — but risks a humanitarian crisis, stains U.S. moral standing, and by no means guarantees regime capitulation.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Infrastructure-wide strikes would remove Iranian export capacity for years without a clear political payoff — a low-reward, high-price-impact branch.
insights.locator: The United States could strike Iranian critical infrastructure

insights.claim: A move to total war would put Gulf states' critical infrastructure, energy and power facilities, civilian population centers and desalination plants at the top of Iran's target list.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: The escalation tail hits Gulf, not just Iranian, assets — relevant to GCC sovereign risk, utilities, desalination and regional insurance pricing.
insights.quote: placing the Gulf states’ critical infrastructure, energy and power facilities, civilian population centers, as well as desalination plants at the top of Iran’s target list
insights.locator: But the cruel logic of this approach is obvious

insights.claim: A ground option would involve seizing Kharg Island, which handles the lion's share of Iran's oil exports, plus securing a strip of Iranian territory adjacent to the Strait of Hormuz for safe transit — putting thousands of U.S. warfighters and prized naval assets at risk.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Kharg Island is the single chokepoint for Iranian crude exports; any move against it is the clearest signal of a shift to a supply-removal scenario.
insights.quote: including to seize Kharg Island—which facilitates the lion’s share of Iran’s oil exports
insights.locator: Trump could also put boots on the ground

insights.claim: Retargeting senior Iranian leaders has limited value because the regime has proved remarkably adept at replenishing itself, if not stiffening its resolve, after such strikes.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Decapitation headlines should not be read as regime-change progress; they historically extend rather than shorten the conflict.
insights.locator: The United States could also begin to re-target senior Iranian leaders

insights.claim: Ray Takeyh and Reuel Marc Gerecht argue Tehran holds a wartime advantage over Washington because the ruling Iranian elite wants to fight and has been willing to endure far more pain than Donald Trump.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Asymmetric pain tolerance means U.S. pressure campaigns are more likely to end in a negotiated fudge than Iranian capitulation.
insights.quote: Tehran has a wartime advantage over Washington because the ruling Iranian elite wants to fight and has been willing to endure far more pain than Donald Trump.
insights.locator: As Ray Takeyh and Reuel Marc Gerecht aptly observed

insights.claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly claims Iran is probably not ready for a deal yet but will be soon because the price it is paying is very high despite its tough talk.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Official U.S. optimism on an imminent deal is the stated administration view — useful as a contrarian marker against the author's stalemate base case.
insights.quote: they’re probably not ready to do a deal yet, but they will be soon because the price they’re paying is very high despite their tough talk and their flowery language

insights.claim: U.S. casualties in the Iran war have reached eighteen service members killed and nearly 450 wounded, including three killed in Iran's recent attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Azraq, Jordan.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Rising casualty counts are the clock on domestic political tolerance — the key variable behind any abrupt U.S. policy shift.
insights.locator: Three U.S. military service members were killed

insights.claim: New polling shows 68 percent of Americans believe the Iran war was not worth fighting, making a continued high-cost campaign politically expensive.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Two-thirds domestic opposition caps the escalation branch and pushes toward a face-saving settlement or frozen conflict.
insights.quote: New polling shows 68 percent of Americans believe the Iran war was not “worth fighting.”
insights.locator: The costs of the war are already high

insights.claim: The war's strategic costs include an accelerated drawdown of munitions already in short supply and the repositioning of forces away from priority theatres such as the Indo-Pacific, which could invite opportunistic Chinese action in the Taiwan Strait.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Direct read-through to defense primes and munitions replenishment budgets, plus a raised Taiwan tail risk while U.S. inventories are drained.
insights.quote: the repositioning of forces from priority theatres, such as the Indo-Pacific, which could invite opportunistic actions from China in the Taiwan Strait
insights.locator: Then there are the strategic costs

insights.claim: Implementing the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding as written would leave Iran able to choke off the Strait of Hormuz at will — or at least charge a toll for passage — while deferring any real discussion of its unresolved nuclear program.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Even the 'deal' scenario leaves a structural Iranian toll or veto over Hormuz transit — a permanent risk premium on Gulf shipping rather than a clean resolution.
insights.quote: Iran would remain in a position to continue to choke off the Strait of Hormuz at will—or at least charge a toll for passage
insights.locator: This option would be a hard sell politically

insights.claim: A unilateral U.S. deescalation would shatter the confidence of regional and other partners in the United States as a trustworthy guarantor of security.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Allied hedging behavior — including regional nuclear and defense diversification — is the second-order cost of a U.S. climbdown.
insights.locator: A unilateral deescalation would also shatter

themes.theme: Stalemate as base case and duration math

insights.claim: The current conflict in the Strait of Hormuz is calcifying into the new status quo: the strait is neither fully open nor closed, the ceasefire is punctuated by near-daily attacks, and oil prices are high but seemingly not crippling to the global economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Base case is a persistent elevated-but-tolerable oil regime with headline volatility, not a resolution or a spike — argues for selling extremes rather than directional bets.
insights.quote: The Strait of Hormuz is neither fully open nor closed.
insights.locator: The Strait of Hormuz is neither fully open nor closed

insights.claim: Applying astrophysicist J. Richard Gott's rule — absent better information, even odds that a phenomenon endures at least as long as it already has — the five-month-old Hormuz stalemate has an even chance of grinding on through the end of 2026, with survival odds improving each additional month.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: A transferable base-rate heuristic for handicapping frozen-conflict duration when no better information exists — useful for sizing multi-quarter risk premia.
insights.quote: absent better information, the odds are even that a phenomenon will endure at least as long as it already has
insights.locator: So, how long could this all last?

insights.claim: Prediction markets put a 50 percent chance on commercial vessel traffic in the Strait of Hormuz returning to normal by the end of 2026, aligning the wisdom of crowds with the Gott-rule estimate.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: A tradable, independently corroborated 50/50 on Hormuz normalization by year-end — a direct benchmark for shipping, tanker rates and oil-curve positioning.
insights.quote: Expectations there put a 50 percent chance on commercial vessel traffic in the Strait of Hormuz “returning to normal” (a proxy for the end of conflict) by the end of 2026
insights.locator: If you don’t find that logic persuasive
